item.title: New Study Explains Double Descent in Deep Learning via Universal Compression
item.description:
New Study Explains Double Descent in Deep Learning via Universal Compression

Researchers have developed a new theoretical framework for understanding the double-descent phenomenon in deep learning models. The study introduces universal compression as a lens to interpret why test loss exhibits a sharp peak near the interpolation threshold before descending again as model size increases.

The double-descent phenomenon has been observed in toy classical models but remains inadequately understood in modern deep learning despite extensive empirical study. This new work upper bounds the maximum-likelihood excess test loss as a sum of four terms: an approximation-and-shift term, a minimax batch regret, a prior cost, and a MLE-vs-Bayes gap.

Experiments reveal that a Gaussian-prior SGLD approximation to the Bayes predictor, unlike SGD, shows no pronounced interpolation peak. Additionally, experiments with uniform random labels support the identified gap as a major contributor to the double-descent peak. At the peak, SGD cross-entropy is roughly four times the SGLD ensemble cross-entropy, while the ensemble cross-entropy remains near log 10.

Under exact posterior sampling, the expected MLE-vs-ensemble gap lower-bounds the MLE-vs-Bayes gap in the well-specified setting.

#DoubleDescent #DeepLearning #UniversalCompression #MachineLearning

Source: Understanding Double Descent through Universal Compression

item.title: Vision Transformer Implementation and Recent Architectural Simplifications
item.description:
Vision Transformer Implementation and Recent Architectural Simplifications

A PyTorch implementation of the Vision Transformer (ViT) demonstrates a simple method for achieving state-of-the-art vision classification using only a single transformer encoder. The significance of the architecture is detailed further in a video by Yannic Kilcher.

🧩 Requirements and Configuration

When configuring the Vision Transformer, specific rules for input dimensions and model parameters must be met:

  • Image Sizing: For rectangular images, set the image size to the maximum of the width and height.
  • Patch Requirements: The image_size must be divisible by patch_size. The resulting number of patches, calculated as n = (image_size // patch_size) ** 2, must be greater than 16.
  • Configurable Parameters:
    • Number of image channels
    • Number of classes to classify
    • Last dimension of output tensor after linear transformation (nn.Linear(..., dim))
    • Number of Transformer blocks
    • Number of heads in the Multi-head Attention layer
    • Dimension of the MLP (FeedForward) layer
    • Dropout rate and embedding dropout rate
    • Pooling method (pool set to either cls token pooling or mean pooling)

⚡ Training Optimizations and Simplifications

An update from several of the original paper’s authors introduces simplifications enabling ViT to train faster and better. Key modifications include:

  • 2D sinusoidal positional embeddings
  • Global average pooling without a CLS token
  • Complete removal of dropout
  • Reduced batch sizes of 1024 instead of 4096
  • Integration of RandAugment and MixUp augmentations
  • A simple linear layer at the end, which performs not significantly worse than the original MLP head

A separate paper proposes leveraging attention and masking flexibility for variable-lengthed sequences to pack images of multiple resolutions into a single batch. This approach achieves faster training and improved accuracy, with the tradeoff of increased architecture and dataloading complexity. It incorporates:

  • Factorized 2D positional encodings
  • Token dropping
  • Query-key normalization

🚀 Framework Availability

The Vision Transformer is available across multiple frameworks and repositories:

Repository / Translation Details
Official Jax Repository Official Jax implementation
PyTorch Pretrained Repository Maintained by Ross Wightman
TensorFlow 2 Translation Created by research scientist Junho Kim
Flax Translation Created by Enrico Shippole

#VisionTransformer #PyTorch #ComputerVision #MachineLearning #DeepLearning

Source: lucidrains/vit-pytorch

item.title: New borscht Framework Releases 12 Progressive AI Models
item.description:
New borscht Framework Releases 12 Progressive AI Models

The SITP.ai repository now hosts the borscht teaching deep learning framework, providing a progression of twelve models from a simple bigram to post‑trained transformers.

🔍 Overview

  • The repository hosts the https://sitp.ai textbook and the borscht teaching deep learning framework.
  • It includes a series of models labeled Model 1 through Model 12.

🧩 Model Progression

Model Type
Model 1 Bigram
Model 2 Discriminative Perceptron
Model 3 Probabilistic Perceptron
Model 4 Multilayer Peceptron
Model 5 Convolutional Neural Network
Model 6 Recurrent Neural Network
Model 7 Long Short-Term Memory Network
Model 8 Encoder-Decoder Pre-trained Transformers (BERT)
Model 9 Decoder Only Pre-trained Transformers (mingpt)
Model 10 Decoder Only Pre-trained Transformers (nanogpt)
Model 11 Post-trained Transformer (nanochat)
Model 12 Post-trained Transformer (nanoreasoner)

⚙️ Technical Details

  • Setup: Run borscht/setup.sh to install Python and Rust toolchains.
  • File 3B: From Managed Python to Native Rust – see pyproject.toml / Cargo.toml.
  • File 3C: From Rust to RISC‑V – see kernelscpu.rs.
  • File 4A: From Rust to CUDA Rust.
  • File 4B: Accelerate Tensor on GPU – python/borscht/tensor_nativegpu.py, rust/kernelsgpu.rs.
  • File 5: Abstracting Acceleration with Dispatcher, Storage, Allocator – see borscht/python/borscht/tensor.py.
  • File 9: From Volta to Ampere (sm80).
  • File 10: From Ampere (sm80) to Hopper (sm90).
  • File 11: Hello Tensor Compiler.
  • File 12: Hello Inference Engine.

📄 Licensing

  • Contributors and authorized researchers retain rights to generate outputs, evaluate models, benchmark, publish research, and explore ideas on equal terms to ordinary users.

🚀 Next Steps

  • After Model 12, the authors suggest reading the research blog series From SITP to SOTA:
    • FS2S Part 1 (ARCH/OPT): From modded‑nanogpt to dsv3 and k3.
    • FS2S Part 1 (SYS): From Hopper to Blackwell and Rubin.

item.title: ROLL: AI Library Enhances LLM Performance

item.title: Sharp approximation theory for deep networks under split spectral norm constraints
item.description:
Sharp approximation theory for deep networks under split spectral norm constraints

Researchers have established a sharp approximation theory for deep ReLU networks operating under a split spectral norm product constraint, addressing limitations in existing statistical estimation methods for noisy data.

🔍 Overview

Deep neural network estimators require stability under input perturbations for applications involving noisy covariates or estimated features. While weight norm constraints are commonly used to control sensitivity by bounding the Lipschitz constant, previous approximation results under fixed bounds on standard norm products were insufficient to establish optimal statistical rates. This new work provides a theoretical framework to address this gap.

🧩 How it works

The study proposes a penalized least squares estimator for deep nonparametric regression. Theoretical results demonstrate that sufficiently smooth Hölder functions can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy as network depth increases, even when the norm-product bound remains fixed. Consequently, the resulting estimator maintains a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant while achieving the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor.

⚙️ Key details

  • Estimator Type: Penalized least squares estimator for deep nonparametric regression.
  • Constraint Type: Split spectral norm product constraint.
  • Function Class: Sufficiently smooth Hölder functions.
  • Performance: Achieves optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor.

💡 Why it matters

The work establishes optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and provides robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations. Numerical studies indicate that the penalized estimator exhibits well-controlled sensitivity to input perturbations and achieves prediction accuracy comparable to classical deep network methods.

#DeepLearning #StatisticalLearning #RobustAI #NeuralNetworks #ApproximationTheory

Source: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants

item.title: TRESS forecasting model retains timestamped recent events for efficient predictions
item.description:
TRESS forecasting model retains timestamped recent events for efficient predictions

A new forecasting model called TRESS (Timestamped Recent Events and Statistical Summaries) addresses the challenge that a fixed number of recent observations may span minutes for one variable and days for another, while earlier measurements can still reveal whether the latest value is unusual for that variable.

🔍 Overview

The proposed model retains the latest observations at their original times and summarises the full history of each variable. For a given set of variables and event budget, this representation stays the same size as the record grows.

🧩 How it works

  • A query-conditioned event lifting module weights deviations from the latest value according to the age of each observation and the forecast horizon.
  • A channel-specific decoder combines the resulting features with historical statistics and a summary shared across variables to predict a correction to the latest value.

⚙️ Key details

  • TRESS retains 8 to 16 observations per variable.
  • On all four benchmarks compared, TRESS records the lowest mean test MSE and MAE among the methods tested.
  • Serving 32 successive query times from one encoded history reduces CPU inference time by a factor of 2.12 to 2.60 across the four datasets.

🚀 Availability

The code for the model is available at the URL provided in the source material.

#Forecasting #MachineLearning #TimeSeries #DeepLearning #Efficiency

Source: TRESS: A Fixed-Size History Representation for Irregular Time Series Forecasting

item.title: Direct Head Architecture Improves Rooftop Solar Capacity Estimation from Imagery
item.description:
Direct Head Architecture Improves Rooftop Solar Capacity Estimation from Imagery

Researchers have proposed Direct Head, a segmentation-guided neural architecture that directly estimates rooftop photovoltaic capacity from aerial imagery without relying on the conventional area-density product approach. The method was evaluated on 7,590 French rooftop installations and shows measurable error reductions compared to parameter-matched baselines.

🔍 Overview

Distribution planners require installation-level inventories of rooftop PV capacity, but interconnection records are often incomplete or spatially aggregated. Conventional image-based estimators address this by segmenting PV arrays, converting the segmentation mask to physical area, and multiplying by an estimated power density — a pipeline that couples capacity prediction to mask-derived area through an area-density product.

🧩 How it works

Direct Head retains U-Net segmentation and soft-mask pooling but departs from the area-density formulation by directly regressing nonnegative capacity from PV-region features and area descriptors. The architecture is segmentation-guided: it uses the spatial evidence from segmentation without requiring capacity to be determined as the product of area and density.

⚙️ Key details

  • Evaluation dataset: 7,590 French rooftop installations
  • Experimental protocol: Three independent runs under the original data split and a department-based holdout
  • Baseline: Parameter-matched area-density neural model
  • Results vs. baseline:
    • Mean absolute error reduced by 8.7% and 12.5% (two holdout conditions)
    • Symmetric mean absolute percentage error reduced by 14.0% and 20.7%
  • Ablation and comparison studies: Controlled architecture variants, auxiliary-loss ablations, conventional estimators, and representative case analyses all support the finding that segmentation provides useful spatial evidence without enforcing an area-density product

#solarPV #capacityestimation #deeplearning #segmentation #energyplanning #computervision

Source: Segmentation-Guided Direct Capacity Estimation of Rooftop Photovoltaics from Aerial Imagery

item.title: New Release 1.0.31: Enhancements and Fixes in AI Model Development
item.description:
New Release 1.0.31: Enhancements and Fixes in AI Model Development

🔍 Overview

The latest release, version 1.0.31, introduces several enhancements and fixes across various AI models, including ViT, EVA, BEiT, NaFlexViT, RepViT, and iFormer. These updates ensure normalization placement and distillation settings are preserved when exporting or reloading models after changing the classifier or pooling.

🧩 How it works

  • Fixes and Improvements:

    • reset_classifier() and checkpoint reconstruction fixes for multiple models.
    • Support for SwiGLU alignment in DINOv3 and Lingbot checkpoints.
    • Preservation of grayscale/non-RGB input channels in data loaders.
    • Layer-wise LR decay grouping fixes for RepViT, HGNet, MViTv2, and pre-norm ViTs.
    • InceptionNeXt feature sizes with output_stride=8/16.

  • New Features:

    • forward_intermediates() and prune_intermediate_layers() support for various models.
    • features_only support for CoaT, ConViT, ConvMixer, CrossViT, and Visformer.
    • prune_head=True removes the whole head, while prune_head=False keeps it.
    • Pruning a hierarchical model to an earlier stage removes the final norm and head sized for the last stage.
    • head_hidden_size is the actual pre-logits (pooled) width in all models.
    • Pool types a model can’t apply now raise at creation / reset instead of being silently ignored or failing in forward.
    • VOLO num_classes=0 output is the class token embedding.
    • Hyperparameter sweeps via a new sweep.py for grid/random search over any train.py argument.
    • WSD sweeps train one stable trunk per hyperparameter combination.
    • train.py enhancements for resuming, stopping, and saving epochs.
    • Add CSPNeXt with ImageNet-1k classification weights converted from OpenMMLab.
    • Foreach steps are chunked by device L2 cache size.
    • RMS update clipping for AdamWLegacy / NAdamW.
    • New decoupled/corrected weight decay NovoGrad variants.
    • Foreach (multi-tensor) impls for RMSpropTF, LaProp, LAMB, LARS, AdaBelief.

⚙️ Key details

  • Model Fixes:

    • reset_classifier() and checkpoint reconstruction fixes for ViT, EVA, BEiT, NaFlexViT, RepViT, and iFormer.
    • Unpooled PiT export and EfficientFormerV2 with distillation disabled.
    • NaFlex: fix ViT / EVA norm placement during conversion.
    • Layer-wise LR decay grouping for RepViT, HGNet, MViTv2, and pre-norm ViTs.
    • InceptionNeXt feature sizes with output_stride=8/16.

  • New Features:

    • forward_intermediates() and prune_intermediate_layers() support for CSPNet, NFNet, DLA, DenseNet, CoaT, ConViT, ConvMixer, CrossViT, HRNet, Inception-v3, Inception-ResNet-v2, NASNet, PNASNet, SelecSLS, SENet, Sequencer2d, VGG, Visformer, Xception, and Aligned Xception.
    • features_only support for CoaT, ConViT, ConvMixer, CrossViT, and Visformer.
    • prune_head=True removes the whole head.
    • prune_head=False keeps the head.
    • Pruning a hierarchical model to an earlier stage removes the final norm and head sized for the last stage.
    • head_hidden_size is the actual pre-logits (pooled) width in all models.
    • Pool types a model can’t apply now raise at creation / reset instead of being silently ignored or failing in forward.
    • VOLO num_classes=0 output is the class token embedding.
    • Hyperparameter sweeps via a new sweep.py for grid/random search over any train.py argument.
    • WSD sweeps train one stable trunk per hyperparameter combination.
    • train.py enhancements for resuming, stopping, and saving epochs.
    • Add CSPNeXt with ImageNet-1k classification weights converted from OpenMMLab.
    • Foreach steps are chunked by device L2 cache size.
    • RMS update clipping for AdamWLegacy / NAdamW.
    • New decoupled/corrected weight decay NovoGrad variants.
    • Foreach (multi-tensor) impls for RMSpropTF, LaProp, LAMB, LARS, AdaBelief.

🚀 Availability

  • Release 1.0.31 is now available with these enhancements and fixes.

💡 Why it matters

These updates ensure better model performance, stability, and flexibility, making it easier for developers to work with various AI models and configurations.

#AI #MachineLearning #ModelDevelopment #DeepLearning #ComputerVision

Source: huggingface/pytorch-image-models

item.title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin Architecture Debuts in MLPerf Training v6.1
item.description:
NVIDIA Vera Rubin Architecture Debuts in MLPerf Training v6.1

NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin architecture has made its debut in MLPerf Training v6.1, showcasing impressive performance and scalability. The new architecture, along with its CUDA software stack, has demonstrated significant advancements in AI training capabilities.

🔍 Overview

  • MLPerf Training v6.1 marks the debut of the NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture.
  • Vera Rubin NVL72 platform delivered the fastest time to train on six of the seven benchmarks.
  • NVIDIA platforms hold the fastest time to train on every benchmark in v6.1.
  • Vera Rubin successfully completed the entire suite in its inaugural run.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved up to 2x more performance than a highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 baseline.
  • For the DeepSeek-V3 671B benchmark, NVIDIA demonstrated massive scale on a 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 cluster.
  • Vera Rubin maintained above 97% overall efficiency when scaling from 256 to 1,024 GPUs.
  • NVIDIA platforms were the only ones to submit results across all seven benchmarks.

🚀 Availability

  • The Vera Rubin architecture is now available and has been tested in MLPerf Training v6.1.

💡 Why it Matters

  • The performance gains span the entire modeling pipeline, supporting everything from large-scale pretraining to reinforcement learning post-training.
  • The new architecture is designed to handle the most demanding workloads, including the 671-billion-parameter token-dropless Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model.
  • The Vera Rubin platform also proved its flexibility by submitting on two different inference backends: NVIDIA NeMo RL with TensorRT-LLM and with vLLM.
  • The NVIDIA Vera CPU is integral to the architecture, sustaining more than 22,500 concurrent RL environments across 256 CPUs in a single Vera CPU rack.

#NVIDIA #VeraRubin #MLPerf #AITraining #CUDA #DeepLearning

Source: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Achieves up to 2x Blackwell Ultra Performance in MLPerf Training v6.1 | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA Introduces cuDLA Python Bindings for Deep Learning Accelerator Workflows
item.description:
NVIDIA Introduces cuDLA Python Bindings for Deep Learning Accelerator Workflows

NVIDIA has introduced the cuda.bindings.cudla module in cuda-bindings 13.3.0 as part of the CUDA Python project. This thin, Cython-generated Python layer exposes the cuDLA C++ API directly to Python, allowing developers to manage NVIDIA Deep Learning Accelerator (DLA) execution without writing C++ runtime code.

🔍 Overview

NVIDIA DLA platforms provide dedicated fixed-function hardware for deep learning inference. On platforms like the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, DLA executes supported neural network operations to offload inference work from the GPU, improving power efficiency and freeing GPU capacity for other application tasks. While DLA does not support as many layers as a GPU, it supports a wide variety of layers used in popular neural network architectures.

🧩 Architecture and API Capabilities

The cuda.bindings.cudla module exposes the runtime API needed for hybrid-mode workflows:

  • API Components: Contains thirteen functions, nine data types, and eight enums for hybrid-mode management.
  • Hybrid Mode Execution: Setting cudla.Mode.CUDA_DLA enables hybrid mode, where DLA tasks are submitted through CUDA streams.
  • Unified Pipelines: CUDA streams coordinate GPU and DLA work so that preprocessing kernels, DLA inference, and postprocessing kernels can be enqueued and executed in order on the same stream.
  • Platform Consistency: The API is identical on Jetson Orin and NVIDIA RTX Spark Windows AI laptops, extending cuDLA execution to mainstream developer laptops.

⚙️ Compilation and Runtime Details

Running DLA workloads requires specific setup and compilation parameters depending on the workflow phase:

Process Step Details Requirements & Behavior
Model Compilation TensorRT trtexec tool compiles a trained model into a DLA loadable Requires TensorRT (example targets TensorRT 11.4.1 with CUDA 13.4 Update 1)
Standalone Mode buildDLAStandalone produces a raw DLA loadable Does not require TensorRT at inference time
Core Selection useDLACore=0 Targets the first DLA engine on Orin
Precision Setting Precision is derived from model tensor types in TensorRT 11 --fp16 and --int8 flags are no longer supported
Model Preprocessing Trimming ONNX graph head and tail layers Necessary when network layers are DLA-incompatible
Layout Selection I/O format options Selects CHW16 layout

🚀 Environment Requirements

  • Runtime Dependencies: To run an existing DLA loadable, only libcudla.so is required. On Jetson Orin, NVIDIA JetPack supplies libcudla.so automatically without requiring a separate cuDLA SDK or extra runtime libraries.
  • Python Version: Python 3.10 is the minimum required version. JetPack’s default Python version may be older than 3.10.

#NVIDIA #CUDA #Python #Jetson #DeepLearning

Source: Run Native DLA Inference in Python on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin Using cuDLA | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA Advances Agentic Inference with Rubin Architecture and NVFP4 Numerical Precision
item.description:
NVIDIA Advances Agentic Inference with Rubin Architecture and NVFP4 Numerical Precision

NVIDIA is advancing its AI factory capabilities through the new Rubin architecture and NVFP4 precision. The company treats AI performance as a co-designed challenge involving GPU architecture, scale-up interconnects, serving software, CPUs, and storage to achieve significant throughput gains for agentic inference.

⚙️ Rubin Architecture and Performance

NVIDIA Rubin increases memory bandwidth significantly while maintaining capacity to optimize the most contested memory tier in AI factories.

  • Rubin memory bandwidth has risen to 19.2 TB/s, while capacity holds at 288 GB of HBM4.
  • The NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of the GB300 NVL72 at 160 tokens per second per user.
  • Each Rubin GPU provides 3.0 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth, enabling approximately 20.7 TB of aggregate HBM4 across a rack.
  • Rubin adds inline memory tensor accelerator (TMA) descriptor updates, allowing one shared descriptor to serve experts with a common layout and reducing metadata overhead.

🧩 NVFP4 Numerical Precision

NVFP4 is a new numerical format that uses a 4-bit E2M1 element with two levels of scaling: an FP8 (E4M3) scale factor for every 16-value micro-block and a per-tensor FP32 scale. It has become the default precision for agentic benchmarks including AA-AgentPerf, SemiAnalysis AgentX, and MLPerf Endpoints.

Metric Benefit of NVFP4
Model Footprint 3.5x reduction relative to FP16; 1.8x reduction relative to FP8
KV Cache Footprint Up to 50% reduction compared to FP8
Resident Context Approximately 2x more context stays on device
Throughput Up to 4x the throughput of an FP8 baseline

🔍 Mixture-of-Experts Scaling

To manage Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models where all expert weights must reside in HBM, NVIDIA utilizes Wide expert parallelism (Wide-EP) through NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM.

  • Wide-EP: Spreads experts across eight or more GPUs. For DeepSeek-R1 at EP64, each GPU holds four experts per layer (232 blocks) instead of the full model.
  • Expert Parallel Load Balancer (EPLB): Redistributes hot and cold experts between forward passes to prevent GPU memory overcommitment.
  • NVLink Interconnect: On GB200 NVL72, 130 TB/s of aggregate NVLink bandwidth absorbs all-to-all dispatch and combine traffic.
  • Performance: Large EP (EP32) delivers up to 1.8x more output tokens per second per GPU than small EP (EP8) at 100 tokens per second per user.

💡 Distributed Serving with Dynamo

NVIDIA Dynamo acts as the distributed serving layer to manage the key-value (KV) cache, which stores intermediate attention calculations from previously processed tokens. The Dynamo router tracks where KV blocks reside and considers both worker load and cached-prefix overlap when placing requests. This architecture leads to higher cache-hit rates during prefill and less bandwidth consumption during decode.

#NVIDIA #Rubin #AIInference #HBM4 #DeepLearning

item.title: NVIDIA TensorRT 11.1 Introduces Global Performance Tuner for Automatic Model Optimization
item.description:
NVIDIA TensorRT 11.1 Introduces Global Performance Tuner for Automatic Model Optimization

The Global Performance Tuner (GPT) is a new feature for automatic performance tuning released in NVIDIA TensorRT 11.1.

🔍 Overview

  • The Global Performance Tuner is a feature for automatic performance tuning released in NVIDIA TensorRT 11.1.
  • It provides automatic, accuracy‑aware and end‑to‑end performance tuning by customizing different optimizations for different models.

🧩 How it works

  • Central design idea: represent alternative scheduling strategies as explicit and searchable build routes.
  • Compiler knob: a configuration setting that changes some aspect of the compilation pipeline (heuristic, fusion decision, or code‑generation path).
    • Each tunable knob exposes a finite set of allowed values and has a default value.
  • Build route: a concrete combination of knob values.
    • When no build route is specified, TensorRT uses the default build route, where every knob retains its default value.
  • Fusion strategies (horizontal vs. vertical) are not universally better; the better route may depend on the model, tensor shapes, and target GPU.
  • Selecting the better route therefore requires building candidate engines for each route, measuring end‑to‑end performance, and choosing the fastest engine that satisfies accuracy requirements.
  • The knob combination is a build‑route specification, not a complete description of the resulting engine; TensorRT still performs later stages such as tactic selection and may reconcile knob values with network constraints.

⚙️ Key details

  • API surface (C++):
    API Description
    bool IBuilderConfig::setBuildRoute(const char* buildRoute); Apply a fixed route to the builder configuration
    const char* IBuilderConfig::getBuildRoute() const; Return the currently specified route
    const char* IBuilderConfig::getAllBuildRoutes() const; Describe the available knobs, their allowed values, defaults, and purposes
  • These APIs can be used to implement custom tuners. A sample C++ implementation is provided in trtexec.
  • trtexec workflow:
    1. User supplies a model and a regex‑like tunable build‑route expression.
    2. The expression is expanded into a list of concrete build routes.
    3. For each route, the model is built, then accuracy and performance are measured.
    4. Routes that crash during building or fail accuracy are excluded.
    5. The engine with the best measured end‑to‑end performance is selected.
  • TensorRT 11.1 provides more than 200 knobs for tuning.
  • The same implementation will be released in Python with Torch‑TensorRT 2.15.
  • Across ten evaluated workloads, tuning delivered performance improvements ranging from 1.14× to 1.63×.

🚀 Availability

  • The Global Performance Tuner ships with NVIDIA TensorRT 11.1.
  • A Python version will be available in Torch‑TensorRT 2.15.

#TensorRT #PerformanceTuning #AIInference #DeepLearning

Source: Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 2 | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Deep Sequence Model Reveals Disrupted Emotion‑Action Coupling in Adolescents with NSSI
item.description:
Deep Sequence Model Reveals Disrupted Emotion‑Action Coupling in Adolescents with NSSI

A new AI study submitted on 8 Oct 2026 combines an experimental pain paradigm, EEG microstate analysis, and an interpretable deep sequence model to uncover neurodynamic mechanisms linking social distress to non‑suicidal self‑injury (NSSI) in depressed adolescents.

🔍 Overview

  • Study population: 106 adolescents with depression (67 with NSSI, labeled DN+; 39 without NSSI, labeled DN-).
  • Conditions examined: social pain, physical pain, and resting‑state.
  • Goal: Identify brain‑state dynamics that differentiate DN+ from DN- during social pain.

🧩 How it works

  • Data acquisition: High‑density EEG recorded while participants experienced social and physical pain stimuli.
  • Microstate analysis: EEG segmented into recurring topographic patterns (microstates) labeled MS3, MS5, etc.
  • Deep sequence model: Integrated disease‑specific, domain‑adversarial, consistency, and contrastive learning objectives to capture higher‑order dependencies in microstate sequences.

⚙️ Key details

  • Classification performance: Social‑pain condition achieved 68.55% accuracy in distinguishing DN+ from DN-, an 8.94‑point improvement over the best baseline.
  • Neurodynamic findings:
    • DN+ adolescents showed weakened bidirectional transitions between MS3 and MS5 during social pain.
    • Source reconstruction linked MS3 to emotional/interoceptive processing and MS5 to action preparation, indicating disrupted emotion‑action coupling.
    • Time‑resolved analysis revealed:
      • Greater early‑to‑middle recruitment of action‑related states.
      • Later recruitment of emotion‑related states in DN+ participants.
  • Mediation patterns:
    • In DN- adolescents, MS5‑to‑MS3 dynamics mediated the link between social‑evaluation sensitivity and affective outcomes.
    • This mediation was absent in DN+ adolescents, while MS3‑to‑MS5 transitions correlated with increased negative affect in DN+.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a mechanistically interpretable neural signature for objective identification of NSSI.
  • Highlights disrupted emotion‑action coupling as a core neurodynamic mechanism in adolescents experiencing social pain.
  • Demonstrates the utility of interpretable deep sequence modeling for uncovering higher‑order brain‑state dependencies in clinical neuroscience.

#NSSI #EEG #DeepLearning #Neuroscience #AI

Source: Social Pain Disrupts Emotion-Action Brain-State Dynamics in Adolescents with Non-Suicidal Self-Injury

item.title: Correlated Expert Placement and Token Shuffling Cut MoE Training Overhead
item.description:
Correlated Expert Placement and Token Shuffling Cut MoE Training Overhead

Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) layers replace the feed‑forward block of a Transformer with E expert networks, routing each token to k experts. When experts are spread across GPUs under expert parallelism (EP), every MoE layer must perform all‑to‑all collectives in both forward and backward passes to dispatch tokens and then combine results.

🔍 Overview

  • On a cluster of 8 AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs per node, all‑to‑all communication can dominate training: 45 % of a step at EP32 with top‑2 routing and 60 % with top‑6 routing.
  • Early in pre‑training, routers already learn correlated expert selection: at top‑2, only 0.8 % of expert pairs in a layer are chosen together, yet they account for 42 % of token assignments, and the experts a token picks in one layer predict its picks in the next layer.

🧩 How MoE Works

  • Expert parallelism (EP) distributes experts across GPUs.
  • Each token is routed to k experts (top‑2 or top‑6 routing are common).
  • All‑to‑all collectives move tokens to the GPUs that host the selected experts, then gather the computed results.

⚙️ Communication Bottleneck

  • The all‑to‑all step is expensive because tokens frequently travel between GPUs and even across nodes.
  • At EP32, the collective alone consumes up to 60 % of the training step (top‑6 routing).

🚀 Optimizations

1️⃣ Correlated Expert Placement

  • Experts that are often selected together are placed on the same GPU.
  • A dispatcher that sends each token to each GPU once removes up to 58 % of dispatched rows.

2️⃣ Token Shuffling

  • When sequence parallelism shards tokens across the EP group, each token is moved during the reduce‑scatter that follows attention to the GPU predicted to hold its next‑layer experts.
  • On a single node this raises the share of token‑expert assignments served locally from 12.5 % to 59 %.

📈 Results

  • Across EP degrees 8‑64 in Megatron‑LM, the two methods together:
    • Reduce all‑to‑all time by 1.16‑2.63×.
    • Reduce end‑to‑end step time by up to 1.41×.
  • Neither optimization alters the model’s routing decisions or expert parameters.

💡 Why It Matters

By exploiting the natural correlated patterns learned by MoE routers, these techniques dramatically cut communication overhead without changing model behavior, enabling faster and more scalable training of large MoE models.

#MoE #GPU #Parallelism #DeepLearning #TrainingEfficiency

Source: Expert Coupling in MoE Pretraining: Reducing All-to-All Overhead with Correlated Placement and Token Shuffling

item.title: AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol using policy network and tree search
item.description:
AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol using policy network and tree search

On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent. AlphaGo won the game, ultimately triumphing 4-1 over Lee Sedol, one of the greatest professional Go players of all time.

🔍 Overview

  • Move 37 in game two of the five‑game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch.
  • The move had a roughly one in 10,000 chance of being made by an expert human player.
  • AlphaGo’s choice was driven by its search machinery, not by the “intuitive” policy network alone.

🧩 How AlphaGo works

  • AlphaGo is made up of two systems.
  • The first, its policy network, was trained to guess what move a strong human would play.
  • The search component explicitly constructed and searched a game tree with thousands of branches, each representing a different possible future.
  • As its reasoning progresses, AlphaGo maintains a record of what it knows about a given position: the game tree, updating it and eventually synthesizing the information to decide which move to make.

♟️ Comparison to Deep Blue

  • When Deep Blue defeated then‑reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, it did so by looking six to eight moves ahead per player and evaluating 200 million chess positions per second, using rules hard‑coded by humans.
  • Go is a vastly more complex game. A stone’s worth depends on how distant groups and territory unfold over dozens of moves. Computing even a fraction of the possible outcomes would take a supercomputer billions of years.

🧠 Cognitive analogy

  • A well‑known theory in the behavioral sciences, popularized by Daniel Kahneman, distinguishes between two modes of human thought: System 1 (fast, gut‑level) and System 2 (slow, deliberative).
  • AlphaGo offered a striking machine analogue of that split: its networks supplied the hunches—this move looks promising, this position looks won—and its search supplied the deliberation, testing those hunches against the moves and countermoves that would follow.

🤖 Contrast with large language models

  • A large language model picks the next token, over and over.
  • Researchers have added chain‑of‑thought prompting so models can generate intermediate steps that decompose a problem, carry forward partial results, and influence subsequent reasoning.
  • The intermediate reasoning is still produced by the same next‑token prediction process, iterated for longer before the model commits to an answer.
  • However, these models typically maintain no explicit, persistent, and inspectable epistemic state; there is no open ledger of hypotheses, confidence, or evidence.
  • Knowledge and reasoning are inextricably interwoven in the weights of the neural network—there is no independent, explicitly represented set of beliefs.
  • Research has shown that bots often concoct chain‑of‑thought explanations after the fact, reaching an answer by one route but reporting another.
  • By contrast, AlphaGo’s game tree provides an explicit, inspectable record of the variations it considered.

📊 Key facts

  • AlphaGo won 4‑1 against Lee Sedol.
  • Move 37 had a ≈1/10,000 chance of being chosen by a human expert.
  • Deep Blue evaluated 200 million positions per second.
  • Go’s outcome space is so large that exhaustive computation would take billions of years on a supercomputer.
  • AlphaGo’s architecture combines a policy network with tree search and a game‑tree data structure.

#AlphaGo #Go #AI #MachineLearning #DeepLearning

Source: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason

item.title: FreNet introduces visual prior‑driven feature reconfiguration for lesion segmentation
item.description:
FreNet introduces visual prior‑driven feature reconfiguration for lesion segmentation

A new framework called FreNet has been introduced to improve medical lesion segmentation by applying visual priors and feature reconfiguration at both pixel and feature levels.

🔍 Overview

  • Lesion segmentation in medical images is critical for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning.
  • Two major challenges hinder accurate segmentation: complex background interference and diverse lesion morphology.
  • Existing encoder‑decoder methods mainly focus on enhancing feature extraction or redesigning decoding strategies, but they lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during the encoding stage.

🛠️ How it works

  • Pixel‑level reconfiguration is performed before the encoding stage to suppress background responses.
  • Feature‑level reconfiguration occurs throughout the encoding stage to better handle varied lesion shapes.
  • The overall pipeline combines these two stages to produce precise lesion masks.

⚙️ Key components

Module Function
Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN) Models a continuous spatial field and leverages visual prior from SAM to reconfigure the input image before encoding.
Dual‑domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) Progressively reconfigures backbone features during encoding.
Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) Decouples backbone features in the frequency domain to enhance foreground‑background discriminability.
Spatial Localization Module (SLM) Relocates features spatially and improves spatial stability after frequency decoupling.

📊 Performance

  • Evaluated on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks spanning three imaging modalities.
  • Demonstrates significant improvements over state‑of‑the‑art (SOTA) methods.
  • On the challenging ETIS dataset, FreNet achieves 5.0 % higher Dice score than the previous SOTA method and 7.2 % higher than SAM.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides early visual‑prior guidance, addressing background interference.
  • Introduces dual‑domain reconfiguration to cope with diverse lesion morphologies.
  • Offers a consistently higher segmentation accuracy across multiple modalities, supporting more reliable clinical decisions.

#MedicalAI #LesionSegmentation #FreNet #DeepLearning #ComputerVision

Source: Feature Reconfiguration With Visual Prior for Medical Lesion Segmentation

item.title: 🚀 PipelineRL: Breaking the Speed-Stability Tradeoff in LLM Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
🚀 PipelineRL: Breaking the Speed-Stability Tradeoff in LLM Reinforcement Learning

𝙎𝙪𝙢𝙢𝙖𝙧𝙮: PipelineRL introduces a groundbreaking approach to LLM reinforcement learning through “inflight weight updates” - continuously updating model weights during inference without stopping generation. This technique elegantly solves the traditional throughput vs. on-policy data collection tradeoff, enabling faster, more stable RL training for large language models.

🔄 Revolutionizing RL Training for LLMs

Reinforcement Learning (RL) with Large Language Models presents a fundamental challenge: how do you balance high inference throughput with on-policy data collection? Traditional approaches force an uncomfortable choice between efficiency and effectiveness. Either you maximize throughput but suffer from stale, off-policy data, or you maintain on-policy learning at the cost of GPU efficiency.

Enter PipelineRL, an experimental open-source implementation that elegantly solves this problem through a surprisingly simple innovation: 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝘄𝗲𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝘂𝗽𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀.

🧠 How PipelineRL Works: Inflight Weight Updates Explained

𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘛𝘳𝘢𝘥𝘪𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭 𝘋𝘪𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘮𝘢

In conventional RL approaches, the process unfolds linearly:

  1. Generate data using the current policy
  2. Update the policy based on this data
  3. Generate new data with the updated policy

This creates significant inefficiencies. To maintain high throughput, inference servers need large batch sizes, generating data for multiple optimization steps at once. But each step increases the lag between the current policy and the inference policy, making collected data progressively less effective.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗥𝗟 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 🔥

PipelineRL’s genius lies in its continuous operation model:

  • Inference servers maintain optimal batch sizes for high throughput
  • Model weights update after each optimizer step 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘱𝘱𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘯𝘧𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦
  • Inference pauses just briefly to receive new weights
  • Sequence generation continues with updated weights, even with “stale” KV caches

The surprising finding? This approach works remarkably well despite theoretical concerns about mixing old KV caches with new model weights!

📊 Empirical Results: Simplicity Beats Complexity

The proof is in the performance. PipelineRL matches or exceeds Open-Reasoner-Zero’s results on reasoning benchmarks like AIME 2024 and MATH 500.

What’s truly impressive is that PipelineRL achieves this with a dramatically simpler implementation. While Open-Reasoner-Zero employs value functions and various stabilization techniques, PipelineRL uses a simplified version of GRPO (Gradient-based Reinforcement Policy Optimization) with:

  • No trust region importance weight clamping
  • No overlong sequence filtering
  • No reward shaping
  • No KL penalty or entropy bonus
  • Simple loss normalization

Despite (or perhaps because of) this simplicity, training remains stable throughout.

🧩 Modular Architecture: Built for Innovation

PipelineRL’s architecture emphasizes modularity, enabling researchers to leverage specialized inference and training software innovations. The system defines clear contracts between components:

𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁

  • Process group initialization
  • Weight update trigger
  • Chat completion API

𝙏𝙧𝙖𝙞𝙣𝙚𝙧 𝘾𝙤𝙣𝙩𝙧𝙖𝙘𝙩

  • Worker initialization
  • Forward pass
  • Backward step
  • Optimizer step
  • Weight gathering and broadcasting

This plug-and-play approach allows researchers to experiment with different inference implementations while maintaining the core PipelineRL advantages.

🔮 Future Directions & Implications

While still experimental, PipelineRL has ambitious plans:

  • 🚀 Implementing coroutines for more precise batch size control
  • 🖼️ Adding multi-modal support
  • ⚡ Developing sequence parallel training

The team emphasizes that PipelineRL aims to be a hackable, fast reference implementation rather than an all-encompassing framework. This philosophy encourages researchers to fork the repository and adapt it to their specific needs.

A forthcoming research paper will provide deeper analysis of how inflight weight updates affect training dynamics and quantify the speed improvements PipelineRL delivers.

🤔 Final Thoughts

PipelineRL represents an elegant solution to a fundamental challenge in RL for LLMs. By updating weights during inference rather than stopping and restarting, it achieves the best of both worlds: high throughput and on-policy learning.

What’s perhaps most interesting is how this approach challenges our assumptions about what “should” work in machine learning. The team found that mixing old KV caches with newly updated weights doesn’t destabilize training as conventional wisdom might suggest.

As LLM training continues to evolve, will we see more innovations that challenge the established “rules” of deep learning? What other tradeoffs might be eliminated through similarly unconventional approaches?

item.title: 🚀 No GPU Left Behind: How Co-located vLLM is Revolutionizing LLM Training Efficiency
item.description:
🚀 No GPU Left Behind: How Co-located vLLM is Revolutionizing LLM Training Efficiency

𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘆: Discover how the new co-located vLLM integration in TRL eliminates idle GPU time during GRPO training by running both training and inference on the same GPUs—delivering up to 1.73× speedup without sacrificing model quality, even on 72B parameter models.

🔍 The Training Bottleneck Problem

Training large language models using online learning methods like GRPO (introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper) requires constant generation of model outputs during the training loop. This creates a critical efficiency challenge: traditional setups force GPUs to take turns between training and inference tasks.

Before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on dedicated GPUs—creating a wasteful “ping-pong” pattern:

  1. Training GPUs run the model update step
  2. Training GPUs sit idle while waiting for generation
  3. vLLM server GPUs generate completions
  4. vLLM GPUs sit idle while training resumes
  5. Repeat…

This inefficient workflow results in:

  • 💸 Wasted GPU resources on both sides
  • 🔌 Increased hardware requirements
  • ⏱️ Reduced overall throughput
  • 📈 Higher training costs

🌟 Enter Co-located vLLM: The Game-Changer

The core innovation introduced in TRL PR #3394 is elegant yet powerful: run both training and inference on the 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 GPUs.

Instead of operating as a standalone server process, vLLM now runs alongside the training code within the same distributed process group. The key advantages of this colocation approach:

  • Unified GPU Utilization: Training and inference share resources, taking turns efficiently without idle time
  • Direct Communication: Eliminates HTTP overhead by running vLLM in-process
  • Seamless Scaling: Works natively with torchrun for multi-node deployment
  • Full Parallelism Support: Compatible with both Tensor and Data Parallelism
  • Simplified Deployment: No separate server management needed

To enable this in your training pipeline, it’s as simple as changing one parameter:

1
2
3
4
5

training_args = GRPOConfig(
 ...,
 use_vllm=True,
 vllm_mode="colocate", # This enables colocation!
)

📊 Real-World Performance Gains

The team ran extensive experiments comparing traditional server mode to the new co-located approach. The results were impressive across various model sizes and configurations:

🔹 For Smaller Models (1.5B parameters)

  • Up to 1.43× speedup with larger batch sizes
  • Better performance with less tensor parallelism

🔹 For Medium Models (7B parameters)

  • 1.35× speedup at larger batch sizes
  • Performance improves with more tensor parallelism, reaching 1.73× speedup

🔹 For Massive Models (Qwen2.5-Math-72B)

  • Co-located setup achieves ~1.26× faster throughput even with 𝙛𝙚𝙬𝙚𝙧 GPUs
  • Equal model quality on Math500 benchmark compared to traditional training

One crucial innovation that enables efficient training of massive models is the integration of vLLM’s sleep() API into the training loop. This function temporarily frees GPU memory, allowing:

  • Level 1 Sleep: Unloads model weights but keeps them accessible in CPU memory
  • Level 2 Sleep: Completely unloads both weights and KV cache

For GRPO, which updates the model after every step, Level 2 sleep provides maximum memory efficiency, avoiding contention between training and generation tasks.

📈 Technical Implementation Details

The implementation combines several advanced techniques to maximize performance:

  1. Process Group Awareness: Co-located vLLM respects the torch.distributed process group:
1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
9

if self.vllm_tensor_parallel_size > 1:
 self.tp_group, _ = torch.distributed.new_subgroups_by_enumeration(
 [
 list(range(i * self.vllm_tensor_parallel_size,
 (i + 1) * self.vllm_tensor_parallel_size))
 for i in range(self.accelerator.num_processes //
 self.vllm_tensor_parallel_size)
 ]
 )

  1. Memory Management: For large models like Qwen2.5-72B, DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 optimizations handle memory constraints:

    • Offloading optimizer states to CPU
    • Overlapping communication with computation
    • Using contiguous gradients to reduce memory fragmentation

  2. Accelerate Integration: The whole system leverages HuggingFace’s Accelerate library for streamlined distributed training.

🔮 The Future of Efficient LLM Training

Despite a few challenges like occasional segmentation faults during shutdown (reported in Issue #16993), the co-located vLLM approach represents a significant advancement in LLM training efficiency.

The most important lessons from this work:

  • 🔥 Co-located inference dramatically improves GPU utilization without requiring additional hardware
  • 🧠 Memory management via vLLM’s sleep() is crucial for large-scale training
  • ⚡ The approach maintains model quality while delivering substantial throughput gains

This innovation makes training large models faster, cheaper, and more accessible—especially important as models continue to grow in size and complexity.

💡 Try It Yourself

Want to experience the efficiency gains firsthand? Here’s a minimal example to get started with GRPO training using co-located vLLM:

 1

from datasets import load_dataset
from trl import GRPOConfig, GRPOTrainer

dataset = load_dataset("trl-lib/tldr", split="train")

def reward_len(completions, **kwargs):
 return [-abs(20 - len(completion)) for completion in completions]

training_args = GRPOConfig(
 output_dir="Qwen2-0.5B-GRPO",
 use_vllm=True,
 vllm_mode="colocate", # Enable colocation
 vllm_gpu_memory_utilization=0.3,
 max_steps=2,

)

trainer = GRPOTrainer(
 model="Qwen/Qwen2-0.5B-Instruct",
 reward_funcs=reward_len,
 args=training_args,
 train_dataset=dataset,
)

trainer.train()

As LLMs become increasingly central to AI advancement, innovations that maximize hardware efficiency will be crucial. The question is no longer just “how powerful is your model?” but also “how efficiently can you train it?”

item.title: Beyond the Algorithm: Decoding Strategies that Make LLMs Shine
item.description:
🧠 Beyond the Algorithm: Decoding Strategies that Make LLMs Shine

Quick Summary: While we often focus on model architectures and training data, the magic of language models also depends on how text is generated. Discover how decoding strategies like greedy search, beam search, and sampling techniques influence the text LLMs produce—and why it matters for your applications.

🔍 The Hidden Decision-Making Behind AI Text Generation

When you marvel at AI’s ability to continue a text prompt, have you ever wondered exactly how it chooses the next word? While researchers obsess over model architectures and training algorithms, there’s a crucial component that often flies under the radar: decoding strategies.

These strategies are the decision-making processes that determine how an LLM selects tokens when generating text. They’re the difference between predictable, repetitive outputs and creative, natural-sounding language.

Let’s say we feed “I have a dream” to an LLM. How does it decide what comes next? The answer lies not in what the model “knows,” but in how it 𝘤𝘩𝘰𝘰𝘴𝘦𝘴.

🎲 The Decoding Toolkit: From Greedy to Nucleus

🏃‍♂️ Greedy Search: The Obvious Choice

Greedy search is exactly what it sounds like—always picking the most probable next token. For our prompt “I have a dream,” it might generate:

  • Most likely token: “of” (17% probability)
  • Next: “being”
  • Next: “a”
  • Next: “doctor”
  • Final: “.”

Result: “I have a dream of being a doctor.”

Simple and efficient? Yes. But also short-sighted. By only considering the single most likely token at each step, greedy search often produces repetitive or predictable text.

⚖️ Beam Search: Considering Multiple Paths

Beam search is more sophisticated—it explores multiple possible continuations simultaneously. Instead of committing to a single token at each step, it keeps track of the top 𝘯 most promising sequences (where 𝘯 is the “beam width”).

Think of it as exploring multiple branching paths, then selecting the one with the highest overall probability. This helps avoid getting stuck in local maxima that might lead to awkward phrasing.

For our example, beam search might produce: “I have a dream. I have a dream”—which, while repetitive, scored higher in overall probability than the greedy search output.

🎯 Top-k Sampling: Controlled Randomness

Top-k sampling introduces an element of creative chance. Instead of always picking the most likely token, it:

  1. Identifies the 𝘬 most probable tokens
  2. Redistributes probability among only these tokens
  3. Randomly selects from this filtered set

With top-k = 20 and our example, we might get: “I have a dream job and I want to”—more natural and less predictable than pure greedy search.

🔬 Nucleus (Top-p) Sampling: Dynamic Flexibility

Nucleus sampling takes a more adaptive approach. Rather than selecting a fixed number of candidate tokens, it:

  1. Sorts tokens by probability
  2. Keeps adding tokens until their cumulative probability exceeds threshold 𝘱
  3. Randomly selects from this “nucleus”

With 𝘱 = 0.5, our prompt might continue as: “I have a dream. I’m going to”

What makes nucleus sampling powerful is its adaptability—when the model is confident, it considers fewer options; when uncertain, it explores more possibilities.

🌡️ Turning Up the Heat: The Temperature Parameter

We can’t discuss decoding strategies without mentioning temperature. This parameter controls the “creativity” of generated text by scaling the logits before applying the softmax function:

softmax(x𝑖) = e^(x𝑖/T) / ∑_j e^(x𝑗/T)

  • Low temperature (T → 0): More deterministic, focused on highest probabilities
  • High temperature (T → 1): More random, distributing probabilities more evenly

Temperature acts as a “creativity knob”—turn it up for brainstorming, down for factual responses.

🔮 Choosing the Right Strategy

Each decoding method offers different tradeoffs:

  • Greedy search: Fast, deterministic, but potentially rigid
  • Beam search: More thorough exploration, but computationally expensive
  • Top-k: Good balance of predictability and variety
  • Nucleus: Adaptive diversity that changes based on model confidence

The best strategy depends on your application:

  • Need factual, consistent responses? → Lower temperature, greedy or beam search
  • Creating creative content? → Higher temperature, nucleus sampling
  • Interactive chat application? → Balanced temperature with nucleus sampling

🚀 Why This Matters

Understanding these decoding strategies gives you powerful control over LLM outputs. By tuning parameters like temperature, beam width, top-k, and top-p, you can dramatically influence the style and quality of generated text—𝙬𝙞𝙩𝙝𝙤𝙪𝙩 retraining or fine-tuning the model.

This knowledge helps explain why the same model can produce wildly different outputs from the same prompt. It’s not just about what the model knows—it’s about how you ask it to express that knowledge.

Next time you’re working with language models, remember that the decoding strategy is your hidden superpower. The choice between greedy shortcuts and explorative sampling might be the difference between a mundane response and a truly insightful one.
